newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-BURNING SKIS AND BITTER COLD IN BORMIO.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-BURNING SKIS AND BITTER COLD IN BORMIO.

text.p: Austria's Werner Franz was fastest in final training for a men's World Cup Alpine skiing downhill on Sunday but the talk at the finish in Bormio on Saturday was of "burning" skis and bitter cold.

Franz, fastest in Friday's sesson and more determined than ever to secure his first World cup win after finishing second at Val d'Isere in the opening downhill, clocked two minutes 01.80 seconds, 0.15 ahead of Italy's Peter Runggaldier.
Organisers said temperatures at the 2,255-metre top of the 3.2 km Stelvio piste were around -18 degrees celsius.
The hard, icy conditions on the demanding downhill effectively divided the racers into two groups -- those whose skis got "burned" and those who escaped unscathed.
"The ice is really doing a lot of damage to the skis," said American racer A.J. Kitt, who was 10th fastest.
"The base, right next to the edges, gets ground away or "burned away" if you slide just a little bit on this ice...it's a really aggressive snow and it really wrecks the skis.
"A couple of guys on our team yesterday went through skis that are wrecked now, they can't use them ever again."
With the base of the skis "burned" away by the ice, racers are forced to ride more on the metallic edges which in turn makes life difficult on the gliding sections.
"Everybody I saw down here today was looking at their edges," said Kitt, the first man down the piste.

Others, including World Cup downhill champion Luc Alphand who complained bitterly here last year about the ice after winning at the World Cup finals in Bormio earlier in 1995, were smiling after their skis passed the test.
The Frenchman, winner of a downhill in Val Gardena and again topping the World Cup downhill standings, clocked the third fastest time just 0.01 behind Runggaldier.
He said afterwards that a new ski base he was using had proved far more resistant to the ice.

Alphand's years of experience and technique were also instrumental, the Frenchman's wiliness symbolised by his red race helmet with a cartoon dog's head on top. "Its an old dog -- the kind that follows the trail best," he joked.
Franz, who uses the same skis as Alphand, said the piste was "brutal" but technical advances in ski design -- with a shock-absorbing plate -- meant the bumps were smoother.
"Nobody could have skied this downhill five years ago," the Ausrian said. "Now its so much fun, its fascinating."
While Franz set the pace for Austria, the rest of the Austrian men had a slower day with only Josef Strobl -- fifth fastest -- finishing in the top 10 in training.

World and former Olympic champion Patrick Ortlieb did not take part because of a stomach problem. Austrian officials said Ortlieb had also been suffering on Friday but he would still be included in the draw.
Austrian Fritz Strobl, winner in Val d'Isere, fell and did not complete the run but he was not hurt.
Three Italians were among the fastest 10, with Runggaldier taking some of the local media attention away from Kristian Ghedina, who won the second Val Gardena downhill.
"He's faster than me today so I can go now," said Ghedina.
